title: Unwell newborn with suspected early-onset sepsis
desc: This station involves a focused history from the midwife and mother and an A to E examination of a 14-hour-old term baby who has become unwell, then interpreting the reassessment, blood gas, blood count, CRP and chest X-ray, outlining the management of early-onset sepsis with shock with doses for this baby, and safety-netting the family.
stem: You are the junior doctor called to the postnatal ward to review a 14-hour-old baby, born at 38+5 weeks with a birth weight of 3.2 kg. The midwife is concerned because the baby has become unsettled, is feeding poorly and is breathing noisily. The mother is at the bedside. The midwife will assist you and give observations when asked.
tasks: Take a focused history from the midwife and the mother and perform a focused examination of the baby using an A to E approach, telling the examiner what you are examining and why. Call for any help you need (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you a reassessment of the baby and the first investigation results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, with doses for this baby, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Roles: the postnatal ward midwife and the mother (one student can voice both, or the examiner voices the midwife). The baby is in a cot under a warmer. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine. The midwife gives the observations and a BGL when asked.

This is an acute station. If the candidate asks for help during Part 1 (calling the neonatal team, oxygen, IV access, a BGL), the midwife says she is doing it and the candidate carries on with the assessment. How the baby responds is given in Part 2. If the candidate has not called for help by halfway through Part 1, the midwife says: "I'm really worried about this baby. Who else should we call?"

Midwife's opening line: "Thanks for coming so quickly. The baby is 14 hours old, has stopped feeding properly and has started grunting. The baby just doesn't look right to me."

Midwife, when asked:

  • Born at 38+5 weeks by normal vaginal birth. Apgar scores 9 and 9, no resuscitation needed. Birth weight 3.2 kg. Vitamin K and hepatitis B vaccine given.
  • Breastfed well twice in the first few hours. Since about 10 hours of age the baby has been sleepy and unsettled, with only brief attempts at the breast and a weak suck.
  • Fast breathing and grunting started about 2 hours ago. No pauses in breathing or blue episodes seen so far.
  • Felt hot to touch in the last hour.
  • Passed urine once and meconium once. One small milky vomit, never green.
  • Mother: GBS positive on the vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks. Labour was quick, and she had one dose of IV benzylpenicillin 2 hours before the birth. Membranes ruptured 20 hours before the birth. Her temperature was 38.2 °C in labour. The liquor was clear and not offensive.
  • The pregnancy was otherwise normal: normal scans, no diabetes, normal antenatal bloods.

Mother, when asked:

  • "The baby was feeding well this morning, but now won't latch and feels hot and floppy."
  • This is your second baby. Your first child is well. You are well yourself now.
  • You thought the baby was just tired after the birth.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are frightened the baby will die, and you wonder whether something you did in labour caused this. You want to keep breastfeeding and to stay with the baby.

Questions to ask if there is time: "Is my baby going to be all right?" "Did I cause this?"
guide:
In Part 1, the midwife and mother answer the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. This is an acute station: credit calling for help, oxygen and access whenever the candidate asks for them, in Part 1 or Part 2. In Part 2, hand over the results and ask the questions in order.

A high-performing candidate recognises sepsis with shock quickly, calls the neonatal team early, checks the BGL, finds every maternal risk factor, gives oxygen and a 32 mL bolus, takes a blood culture and gives benzylpenicillin and gentamicin with correct doses without delay. They interpret the gas, neutropenia, early CRP and chest X-ray correctly, plan neonatal unit care with a 48-hour antibiotic review, speak to the mother with honesty and empathy, and give specific safety netting including late-onset GBS and future pregnancies.

A borderline candidate recognises that the baby is unwell but escalates late, misses the BGL or a risk factor, cannot give doses, is reassured by the low CRP, or gives a limited explanation and vague safety netting.
explain:
Early-onset neonatal sepsis

Sepsis in the first 72 hours is usually from maternal flora, most commonly Group B streptococcus and E. coli. Risk factors include maternal GBS carriage, inadequate intrapartum antibiotics (less than 4 hours before birth), prolonged rupture of membranes (18 hours or more), maternal fever and prematurity. This baby has four of them.

Recognition and stabilisation

Signs include grunting, tachypnoea, tachycardia, poor perfusion (CRT 3 seconds or more), temperature instability, lethargy and poor feeding. Call the neonatal team early. Give oxygen for SpO2 below 92%, obtain IV or IO access, give a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus (32 mL for 3.2 kg) and reassess, check the BGL, take a blood culture and give antibiotics without delay: benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg (192 mg) and gentamicin 5 mg/kg (16 mg) for this baby, as the RCH neonatal dosing guidance sets out. Maintenance fluid on day 1 is 10% glucose at 60 mL/kg/day (8 mL/h).

Interpreting the results

The reassessment shows a response to oxygen and fluid, but the baby is still unwell. The metabolic acidosis with a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L reflects poor perfusion. Neutropenia in a septic newborn is a worrying sign. CRP rises over 12 to 24 hours, so a low early value does not exclude sepsis. The chest X-ray fits pneumonia; GBS pneumonia can look like surfactant deficiency. Blood culture is the key test, and a lumbar puncture is done once the baby is stable.

Disposition and safety netting

The baby needs neonatal unit care. Escalate apnoea, a rising oxygen need, recurrent shock after two boluses, hypoglycaemia or seizures. Antibiotics are reviewed at 48 hours with the culture result. The mother is supported to stay close and provide breast milk. Before discharge, parents are told the signs of late-onset infection, which can occur in the first 3 months, and the mother is offered intrapartum antibiotics in any future pregnancy.
points: Treat suspected early-onset sepsis urgently: blood culture, then benzylpenicillin and gentamicin as per RCH neonatal dosing, without delaying treatment.
Compensated shock in a neonate (HR above 160, CRT 3 s or more, raised lactate) needs a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus with reassessment and a BGL check.
A normal early CRP does not exclude sepsis; repeat at 12 to 24 hours and review antibiotics at 48 hours.
Communicate honestly with the mother, reassure that GBS carriage is common, and support breast milk expression and bonding.
refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical practice guidelines and neonatal dosing guidance for neonatal sepsis.
Safer Care Victoria. Maternity and Newborn eHandbook: Group B streptococcus and early-onset neonatal sepsis.
Australian and New Zealand Committee on Resuscitation (ANZCOR). Guideline 13: Neonatal resuscitation.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self to the mother and midwife, and works in a calm, organised way.
Uses plain language with the mother, acknowledges her fear and keeps her informed.
History
Characterises the illness:

kids.x: Onset of sleepiness, poor feeding and a weak suck from about 10 hours of age
Fast breathing and grunting, and any pauses in breathing or colour change
Urine and meconium passed, and vomiting (whether green)

check.x: Identifies the risk factors for early-onset sepsis:

kids.x: Intrapartum antibiotics given less than 4 hours before birth (inadequate)
Membranes ruptured 18 hours or more before birth (20 hours)

check.x: Asks about the birth and the baby's condition after it: gestation, mode of birth, Apgar scores and any resuscitation, and feeding method.
Explores the mother's ideas, concerns and expectations.
Examination
Observes colour, tone, activity and cry: pale, mottled, floppy, weak cry, responds to voice only.
Assesses breathing: RR 74, grunting, recession and nasal flaring; asks for SpO2 (91% in room air) and listens to the chest (fine crackles at the bases).
Assesses circulation: HR 188, central CRT 4 seconds, cool mottled peripheries, weak peripheral pulses and BP 58/30.
Checks the BGL straight away and states that 4.1 mmol/L is normal (2.6 mmol/L or above).
Measures the temperature (38.1 °C), undresses the baby fully and checks the fontanelle, skin for rash, umbilicus, abdomen, tone and primitive reflexes.
Interpretation
Recognises sepsis with compensated shock and respiratory distress from Part 1: HR above 160, CRT 3 seconds or more, mottling, grunting, SpO2 below 92%, fever and reduced responsiveness.

Interprets the reassessment: the baby has responded to oxygen and one bolus (SpO2 95%, HR 164, CRT 2 seconds) but remains unwell and needs close reassessment, with a further bolus if shock signs return.
Interprets the gas as a metabolic acidosis with a raised lactate (pH 7.24, base excess -9, lactate 4.2) from poor perfusion.
Interprets the blood count: a low white cell count and neutropenia support sepsis and are a worrying sign, and the platelets are slightly low.
States that a CRP barely above normal this early does not exclude sepsis, as CRP rises over 12 to 24 hours, and plans a repeat.
Interprets the chest X-ray as consistent with pneumonia (GBS pneumonia can look like surfactant deficiency) and names the likely diagnosis: early-onset sepsis, probably GBS, with pneumonia.
Considers other causes: transient tachypnoea or surfactant deficiency, duct-dependent congenital heart disease, and an inborn error of metabolism, and says that none should delay antibiotics.
Management
Calls the neonatal registrar or NICU team early, using a structured handover (ISBAR).
Gives oxygen because SpO2 is below 92%, targeting 92 to 96%, and escalates respiratory support (CPAP) if the baby tires, has apnoea or needs more oxygen.
Obtains IV or IO access and gives 0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg = 32 mL for 3.2 kg, reassesses HR and CRT, and repeats 10 mL/kg (32 mL) if still shocked.
Takes a blood culture without delaying treatment, then gives IV benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg = 192 mg for 3.2 kg (12-hourly) and gentamicin 5 mg/kg = 16 mg for 3.2 kg (24-hourly) straight away.
Starts maintenance IV fluid with 10% glucose at 60 mL/kg/day on day 1 = 8 mL/h for 3.2 kg, and plans repeat BGLs.
Admits to the neonatal unit with continuous monitoring, plans a lumbar puncture once stable, repeats the CRP, and reviews antibiotics at 48 hours with the culture result.

Explains to the mother in plain language that the baby probably has a blood and lung infection, needs antibiotics, oxygen and fluids in the neonatal unit, that GBS carriage is common and not her fault, and that she can stay close and express breast milk.
Safety netting
States the triggers for urgent senior review in the unit: apnoea or a rising oxygen need, shock signs returning after two boluses (inotropes are then considered), a low BGL, or seizures.

Tells the parents that after discharge they should return to the ED, or call 000 if the baby is floppy, blue or not breathing normally, for poor feeding, sleepiness, a temperature of 38 °C or more or a low temperature, fast or noisy breathing, or fewer wet nappies, because late-onset GBS infection can occur in the first 3 months.

Arranges follow-up: GP and maternal and child health review after discharge, and tells the mother and her obstetric team that in a future pregnancy she will be offered antibiotics in labour because this baby had GBS infection.

part2.lead: Here is the reassessment 20 minutes later, on oxygen and after one 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride, and the first results. The blood culture was taken before antibiotics.

handover.label: Reassessment 20 minutes later
handover.result: On low-flow oxygen by nasal prongs, after one 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride (32 mL): SpO2 95%, RR 66 with less grunting, HR 164, CRT 2 seconds, BP 62/36, temperature 38.0 °C, still responds to voice only. Repeat BGL 3.9 mmol/L.

ask: What do the reassessment and the results show?
What is the most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider?
What is your management now? Give drugs and fluids with doses for this baby.
Where will the baby be cared for, and what will you tell the mother?
What would make you escalate further, and what follow-up and advice will the family need?
